title: Is Looking Forward to Something Better Than the Thing Itself?
metaTitle: Is Anticipation Better Than the Thing Itself?
metaDescription: Anticipation is a real and underrated source of happiness — sometimes bigger than the event itself. Here is what the research shows, and the catch.
keyFinding: Anticipation is a genuine and underrated source of happiness — for some events the biggest wellbeing boost comes before the thing happens — though expecting too much can turn looking forward into letdown.
honestAnswer: Sometimes, yes — anticipation is a real and underrated source of happiness, and for some experiences the looking-forward part delivers more than the event itself. The pleasure of an upcoming trip, meal, or reunion is not just a preview of the real thing; it is its own distinct enjoyment, and research suggests it can be surprisingly large.

There is a catch worth stating up front: anticipation can also breed letdown if your expectations climb too high, so it is not a free win. But on balance, looking forward to things is a genuine, stretchable source of wellbeing that most people underuse — and one worth deliberately building into how you plan your time and spending.
whatDataShows: Research on vacations is the clearest example. Studies in this area, including work by de Bloom and colleagues, found that the largest wellbeing boost from a holiday often comes from the anticipation beforehand rather than from the afterglow once you are home — vacationers tend to be measurably happier in the run-up than their post-trip levels would predict, and the lift afterward often fades quickly. In other words, a sizeable share of a trip's happiness value is paid out before you ever leave.

How you spend also shapes how good the anticipation feels. Research by Van Boven and Gilovich found that people derive more happiness from experiential purchases than material ones, and follow-up work by Kumar, Killingsworth and Gilovich found that waiting for an experience produces more pleasurable, less impatient anticipation than waiting for a possession. We savor the upcoming concert or holiday in a way we rarely savor the upcoming gadget — the wait itself is more enjoyable.

The broader mechanism is savoring: anticipation lets you enjoy an experience twice, once in imagination before it happens and again in the living of it (and arguably a third time in memory afterward). Because the imagined version is unconstrained by logistics, weather, or fatigue, the anticipatory enjoyment can be remarkably pure — which is part of why it sometimes outshines the real event.
whyItFeelsDifferent: We tend to treat the event as the "real" thing and the waiting as mere preamble, so we discount the happiness the wait is quietly providing. The days of looking forward to something don't feel like part of the experience, even though research suggests they often carry as much or more of its emotional payoff.

There is also an asymmetry between experiences and things. Waiting for a possession tends to feel impatient — you just want it to arrive — while waiting for an experience tends to feel pleasurable, full of imagining and planning. Because so much modern consumption is material and instant, we get a lot of practice with impatient waiting and comparatively little with the savoring kind, which makes the value of anticipation easy to miss.

And the highlight-reel culture trains us to focus on the moment of arrival — the photo at the destination, the unboxing, the milestone hit — not on the long, pleasant stretch of looking forward to it. So the part of happiness that is most reliably available, and most under your control, is the part we are least encouraged to notice.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Build anticipation in deliberately. Booking experiences in advance rather than last-minute gives you a longer runway of looking forward, which the research suggests is a genuine source of wellbeing in itself — so the gap between booking and going is a feature, not wasted time. Spacing pleasures into the future and letting yourself plan and imagine them extends their total enjoyment.

Favor experiences over things where you can, and lean into the wait. Because experiential purchases produce more pleasurable, less impatient anticipation, choosing the trip or the class over the object tends to pay an anticipation dividend on top of the experience itself. Talking about, planning, and imagining the upcoming experience is part of how that value gets realised.

Use savoring as a skill. Deliberately attending to an upcoming experience — picturing it, planning the details, letting yourself enjoy the prospect — is a documented way to draw more happiness from it. The same applies afterward through memory, which means a well-chosen experience can pay out three times: before, during, and after.
whatDoesNotHelp: Inflating your expectations does not help, and is the main way anticipation backfires. If you build an event up into something that has to be perfect, the gap between the imagined version and the real one can produce disappointment that cancels out the anticipatory gain. Looking forward to something is most valuable when the expectations stay realistic rather than escalating.

Spontaneity-for-its-own-sake, with nothing ever planned ahead, forfeits the anticipation entirely. Last-minute everything may feel free, but it skips the looking-forward stage that research suggests carries a real share of an experience's happiness — so always-instant gratification can quietly leave wellbeing on the table.

And waiting for material purchases is not the same lever. The pleasurable-anticipation effect shows up much more strongly for experiences than for things; counting on the wait for a new possession to deliver the same savoring tends to disappoint, because waiting for objects usually feels impatient rather than enjoyable.
realNumbersInContext: The headline pattern, from research on holidays including de Bloom and colleagues, is that the largest happiness boost often arrives before the trip rather than after it — anticipation can outweigh the afterglow. The exact size varies by study and by person, and not every event follows the pattern, so treat it as a robust tendency rather than a guarantee that the wait always beats the event.

On the spending side, the consistent finding (Van Boven and Gilovich; Kumar, Killingsworth and Gilovich) is directional: experiential purchases tend to generate more pleasurable and less impatient anticipation than material ones. These are modest effects rather than dramatic ones, and the practical takeaway is simple — anticipation is a genuine, stretchable source of happiness that is largely free and under your control, as long as you keep expectations from running away.

keyTakeaways: For some experiences the largest happiness boost comes before the event, in the anticipation, not after it.
Waiting for an experience feels more pleasurable and less impatient than waiting for a possession.
Savoring lets you enjoy an experience twice — in imagination beforehand and again in the living of it.
The main way anticipation backfires is inflated expectations; it pays off best when they stay realistic.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: A trip booked three months out
examples.body: Reserving a holiday well in advance can feel like a long, pointless wait for the 'real' thing. But the research on vacations, including de Bloom and colleagues, suggests those weeks of looking forward often carry a sizeable share of the trip's happiness — a lift that can outweigh the afterglow once you're home. The gap between booking and going isn't wasted time; it's the anticipation dividend paying out.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: The concert versus the gadget
examples.body: Waiting for a new phone tends to feel impatient — you just want it to arrive. Waiting for an upcoming concert tends to feel pleasurable, full of imagining and planning. Same waiting period, very different experience, which is the experiences-over-things asymmetry in miniature: choosing the concert pays an anticipation dividend on top of the event itself.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: The reunion built up too high
examples.body: Looking forward to a long-awaited reunion is a real source of pleasure — until the imagined version has to be flawless. If expectations climb until only a perfect evening will do, the gap between the picture and the reality can produce a letdown that cancels the anticipatory gain. The lever works best when the looking-forward stays warm but the expectations stay grounded.

pullQuotes.text: A sizeable share of a trip's happiness value is paid out before you ever leave.

faqs.question: Is anticipation really a bigger source of happiness than the event?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Research on vacations, including work by de Bloom and colleagues, found the largest wellbeing boost often comes from anticipation before the trip rather than the afterglow afterward. It varies by event and by person, so treat it as a strong tendency rather than a rule — but looking forward is a genuine source of happiness in its own right.

faqs.question: Why does looking forward to experiences feel better than waiting for things?
faqs.answer: Research by Van Boven and Gilovich and by Kumar, Killingsworth and Gilovich found that waiting for an experience produces more pleasurable, less impatient anticipation than waiting for a possession. We savor an upcoming trip or concert in a way we rarely savor an upcoming object — the wait itself is more enjoyable.

faqs.question: How can I use anticipation to be happier?
faqs.answer: Book experiences in advance to give yourself a longer runway of looking forward, favor experiences over things, and let yourself plan and imagine the upcoming event. The gap between booking and going isn't wasted time — it's part of the enjoyment. Just keep expectations realistic so the wait doesn't set up a letdown.

faqs.question: Can looking forward to something backfire?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you inflate your expectations and build an event into something that has to be perfect, the gap between the imagined version and the real one can produce disappointment that cancels the anticipatory gain. Anticipation pays off best when expectations stay realistic rather than escalating.

faqs.question: What does it mean to 'savor' an experience twice?
faqs.answer: Anticipation lets you enjoy an experience once in imagination before it happens and again in the living of it — and arguably a third time in memory afterward. Because the imagined version isn't constrained by logistics or fatigue, the anticipatory enjoyment can be especially pure, which is part of why it sometimes outshines the event.

dataSources: de Bloom, J., et al. — research on vacations and wellbeing, including the finding that anticipation before a trip can exceed the post-trip boost (e.g., Nawijn, J., et al. (2010). Vacationers Happier, but Most not Happier After a Holiday. Applied Research in Quality of Life).
Van Boven, L., & Gilovich, T. (2003). To Do or to Have? That Is the Question. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(6), 1193–1202.
Kumar, A., Killingsworth, M. A., & Gilovich, T. (2014). Waiting for Merlot: Anticipatory Consumption of Experiential and Material Purchases. Psychological Science, 25(10), 1924–1931.
Bryant, F. B., & Veroff, J. — research on savoring as a way to extend the enjoyment of experiences.
